messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 34

He is a 48-year-old Middle Eastern man who lives alone now, after a divorce that he describes as “another kind of aftermath.” He works as a fashion designer, a profession that once felt playful and exacting in the best way, but which now carries a strain of vigilance he did not know before the disaster. In sessions, he tells his story as if he is still trying to arrange the pieces in a way that makes sense.

The traumatic event began as a normal workday in the city, where he had gone to meet a supplier and review fabric samples for an upcoming collection. He remembers the heat, the noise of traffic, the usual impatience of people moving through narrow streets. Then there was the explosion. He does not speak of it dramatically; instead he describes the moment in fragments: a sudden pressure in his chest, a white flash, the sensation that the ground had tipped. Windows shattered. Smoke filled the air. People screamed. For a few seconds he could not understand what was happening, and then he saw bodies on the pavement and a man calling for his mother in a voice that he says still wakes him at night.

What stays with him most is not only the blast itself, but the confusion that followed. He had been on his way to work, thinking about color palettes and hem lines, and suddenly he was running with others, ducking behind damaged cars, helping a woman whose face was bleeding from glass. He remembers the smell of dust, metal, and burning fabric. He says that one of the hardest parts was realizing how quickly ordinary life can become unrecognizable. Afterward, he walked for hours before he could return home, unable to call anyone because his phone had died and because, as he puts it, “I did not know what language to use for what I had seen.”

In the weeks that followed, sleep became broken and shallow. He began waking at the slightest noise, his body already braced before he was fully aware. Sirens in the street or a slammed door can bring back the same surge of panic he felt that day. He does not describe full scenes so much as flashes: the dust cloud, the ring in his ears, a hand reaching out from beneath debris. These images intrude while he is eating, while he is drafting sketches, while he is trying to answer emails. He notices himself scanning exits in restaurants and sitting with his back to walls. Crowds make him tense; he avoids markets and crowded avenues unless he has no choice. Even then, he moves quickly and with obvious strain.

His work has changed in quiet ways. He still designs, but his process is slower and more cautious. He says that before the attack, he could spend hours in a studio full of chatter and music. Now he prefers silence, and he often works alone. The sound of fabric cutting, once satisfying, can abruptly remind him of debris and torn material. He has thrown away samples when the smell of smoke seemed to rise from them, though no one else could detect it. He has also become preoccupied with control, arranging tools and materials in precise order, as if neatness might protect him from chaos. He is still talented and attentive to detail, but the ease he once brought to his craft has been replaced by strain.

His divorce occurred during the months after the disaster, when he became more withdrawn and less available at home. He says his ex-wife told him he was “always elsewhere,” and he cannot entirely disagree. He was irritable, often startled, and at times emotionally distant in a way that felt alien even to him. He avoided talking about the bombing because whenever he started, he felt heat rise in his chest and his throat close. Over time, he noticed he was less interested in social gatherings, less able to imagine a future that felt stable. He remains loving toward his adult children, though he admits he calls them more often than he sees them, as if distance is safer.

Now he lives with a persistent sense that danger is close, though he knows this is not always rational. Some days he can move through the city with relative calm; on others, a sudden noise or the sight of broken glass is enough to pull him back into the memory of the blast. He feels guilty that he survived when others did not, especially those he tried to help and could not save. At the same time, he speaks with care about the life he has rebuilt, one measured step at a time. He continues to design, to sketch, to choose colors, but he does so with the knowledge that the world can change in an instant, and that part of him remains alert for the next moment when it does.
